newsitem.title: USA: Fed deeply divided at May 20 session on rates.
newsitem.headline: Fed deeply divided at May 20 session on rates.

text.p: Federal Reserve policymakers were deeply divided at their May 20 session over whether to raise interest rates, but ultimately decided to hold policy steady, minutes of the meeting released on Thursday showed.

The vote in favor of steady policy was 9-1 with Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus dissenting in favor of higher rates to counter inflation. Some other policymakers also argued for tighter credit but ultimately agreed to wait.
The policymakers, though, did unanimously agree to bias future potential interest-rate moves in the direction of tighter credit.

"Such a bias ... was consistent with the members' view that the risks were in the direction of a potential need for some tightening ... and that they might be required to make such a decision in the not-too-distant future," the minutes said.

The Federal Open Market Committee met again on Wednesday, once again keeping rates unchanged. The last time the U.S. central bank raised rates was on March 25, when it bumped up the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point.
The May 20 minutes showed that FOMC members were surprised and puzzled by the benign behavior of inflation, especially given the low rate of unemployment.

The government said on Thursday that the unemployment rate rose to 5 percent in June from a 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May. That sparked a surge in bond and stock prices as investors bet the Fed will continue to hold off from raising rates.
At the May 20 meeting, the FOMC continued to voice concern about the risk of "some upturn" in inflation, "perhaps sooner rather than later."

The policymakers forecast that economic growth was likely to slow to a pace at or a little above long-run potential. But they were nevertheless worried that such a slowdown would not necessarily contain inflation.

Those FOMC members arguing for steady rates on May 20 pointed to slowing growth and the absence of higher inflation as justification for a cautious policy stance. They also noted that real interest rates were not unusually low.
But they nevertheless "agreed that some tightening might well be needed later to contain potentially rising inflation," the minutes said.
Other FOMC members who preferred tighter credit in the near term argued that a small rate rise would offer little risk of thwarting expansion but might head off the threat of higher inflation.
Broaddus dissented from the majority, in particular because of the strength of investment demand at a time when the economy alrady was running at a high level and the labor market was very tight.
